words.meaning: false information that spreads, regardless of intent

words.meaning: to divide people into sharply opposing groups

words.meaning: to keep reading bad news online in a compulsive way

words.meaning: a fake video or audio made with AI to look and sound real

words.meaning: causing a strong habit that is hard to break
words.example: Social media apps are deliberately designed to be addictive.

words.meaning: to make someone less sensitive to shocking things
words.example: Endless violent footage can desensitize viewers to real suffering.

words.meaning: a subtle difference in meaning, tone, or expression
words.example: Machine translation still misses the nuance of literary language.

words.meaning: a statement that seems contradictory but may contain truth
words.example: There is a paradox at the heart of social media: it connects us yet leaves us lonelier.

words.meaning: to gradually wear away or weaken something
words.example: Constant interruptions gradually erode our ability to concentrate.

words.meaning: spreading widely through every part of an area or group
words.example: Advertising has become so pervasive that we barely notice it anymore.

words.meaning: to make something less severe or serious
words.example: Tech companies claim new filters will mitigate online harassment.

words.meaning: responsibility for one's actions, with an obligation to explain them
words.example: There must be greater accountability for how platforms handle personal data.

words.meaning: resembling a totalitarian state with extreme surveillance and control
words.example: The proposal for mandatory location tracking struck many as orwellian.

grammar.title: Conditionals type 2 and 3
grammar.explanation: Conditional sentences describe what happens, or what would happen, under certain conditions. Type 2 and Type 3 both imagine situations that are not real — but they differ in time. Second conditional talks about an unreal present or future: something unlikely or impossible right now. Form: If + past simple, would + base verb. Note that after if we use were for all persons: If I were you, I would disconnect for a week. Third conditional talks about an unreal past: something that already happened differently, so it cannot be changed. Form: If + past perfect, would have + past participle. It often expresses regret or criticism: If the platform had moderated the content, the rumor would not have spread. A common mistake is mixing the forms. The if-clause never takes would: If I would have known is incorrect — say If I had known.
examples: If algorithms were fully transparent, users would trust them more.
If I were the minister, I would ban facial recognition in public spaces.
If the company had disclosed the breach earlier, it would have avoided the scandal.
If social media had never been invented, our attention spans would have remained intact.
If governments regulated AI today, innovation would slow down — but safety would improve.
If she hadn't doomscrolled all night, she wouldn't have felt so anxious this morning.
